questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Halden & Pierce, a consulting firm that sells prepaid advisory-hour packages and workshop seats to small businesses, is building a customer support resolution agent with the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests such as refunds for unused hours, billing disputes, and portal account issues through custom MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human), and the target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. The main agent delegates refund-eligibility checks to an eligibility subagent through the Task tool, with prompts such as "Check whether the customer we just discussed qualifies for a refund on the order they mentioned." The subagent replies with generic policy text or asks which order is meant, and when it is invoked again for a second order in the same chat, it works out the policy from scratch. A developer proposes keeping the short prompts and giving the subagent a fixed name, "eligibility-agent", so that it can build up memory across calls. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Reject it: the subagent sees neither the main conversation nor its own earlier calls, so each Task prompt must carry the tier, order ID, dates, and prior result.
Accept it, and add a line to the AgentDefinition system prompt telling the subagent to consult its earlier invocations, so that the fixed name actually has an effect.
Reject it, and let the subagent call get_customer and lookup_order on every invocation, so that it rebuilds the customer and order context from the backend by itself.
Accept it, and have the main agent ask the customer to restate the order number before each delegation, so that the subagent always works from fresh input.
questoes.explicacao: Subagents spawned with the Task tool start with only what their prompt contains: they do not inherit the parent conversation and do not share memory between invocations, whatever they are named. "The customer we just discussed" refers to context the subagent never receives. The main agent must pass the customer's tier, the order ID, the relevant dates, and any earlier eligibility result explicitly in each Task prompt.
feedbacks: Correct. Subagents do not inherit the parent's context or share memory between invocations; everything they need goes in the Task prompt.
Naming a subagent does not give it memory; an instruction to consult earlier invocations points at context it never receives.
The subagent still does not know which customer or order is meant, and repeating lookups duplicates work the main agent already did.
Pushes the burden onto the customer and hurts first-contact resolution; the restated number lands in the parent conversation, which the subagent cannot see.

questoes.pergunta: At Halden & Pierce, closed support conversations are also checked by a Claude-based quality reviewer that flags issues for support leads in four categories: wrong refund amount, missed escalation, unverified identity, and tone. Last month, 68% of tone flags were dismissed as wrong, and a survey shows that leads now skim past the whole queue, including refund-amount flags that are accurate 93% of the time and caught $18,400 in errors. The team has one sprint before the quarterly audit. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Add an instruction to the reviewer prompt to report only issues it is highly confident about, so that the number of flags in the queue drops for each category.
Sort the queue so that refund-amount flags appear first and tone flags appear last, so that leads see the most reliable categories before they stop reading.
Switch off the tone category for now while its criteria are rewritten, so that leads can rely on the queue again and act on the flags that are still accurate.
Have a second Claude instance re-check each flag before it reaches the queue, so that false positives in the four categories are filtered out automatically.
questoes.explicacao: One category with a high false positive rate erodes trust in the whole queue, so accurate refund-amount flags are being ignored along with bad tone flags. Temporarily disabling the noisy category restores trust quickly while its criteria are improved, and the valuable categories keep working. Confidence wording, sorting, or an extra review layer leave the source of the noise in place.
feedbacks: Confidence-based filtering such as "only report high-confidence issues" does not improve precision the way specific criteria do, and it would also cut into the accurate categories.
Sorting changes what leads see first but keeps a mostly wrong category in the queue, so the trust problem that makes leads skip everything remains.
Correct. Temporarily disabling the high false positive category restores trust in the accurate ones while its prompt is fixed with explicit criteria.
Over-engineered for a one-sprint fix: it doubles cost and latency and still asks a model to judge "tone" without the explicit criteria that are actually missing.

questoes.pergunta: Halden & Pierce's engineers build the support agent with Claude Code and want every developer who clones the repository to get the staging CRM MCP server automatically. A pull request that adds the server to the project's .mcp.json is blocked by the secret scanner because the CRM API token is written inline in the server's env block. Each developer already has a personal staging token. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Move the server definition into each developer's ~/.claude.json with their own token, so that no credential appears in a file committed to the repository.
Keep the server in .mcp.json but add the file to .gitignore and share a template on the wiki, so that each developer fills in their token locally.
Store the token in the project CLAUDE.md under a credentials section, so that Claude Code can supply it to the server when the connection starts.
Keep the server entry and reference the token as ${CRM_API_TOKEN} instead, so that each developer's own environment provides the value at startup.
questoes.explicacao: Project-scoped .mcp.json is the right place for a server the whole team shares, and it supports environment variable expansion. Replacing the literal token with ${CRM_API_TOKEN} keeps the shared configuration in version control while each developer's credential stays in their own environment. Moving or ignoring the file gives up the shared, versioned configuration that was the goal.
feedbacks: User-level ~/.claude.json is for personal or experimental servers; it avoids the secret but forces every developer to configure the shared server by hand, which defeats the goal.
Ignoring .mcp.json removes it from version control, so new clones no longer get the server automatically and the wiki template drifts from the real configuration.
CLAUDE.md holds instructions and project context, not credentials; it is also committed, so the token would still be exposed in the repository.
Correct. Environment variable expansion in .mcp.json shares the server configuration through the repo without committing anyone's token.

questoes.pergunta: In Halden & Pierce's support agent, a customer writes: "This is the second time you've billed me twice for the same workshop seat. Honestly, your billing is a mess." lookup_order confirms a duplicate $240 charge, and refunds of that size are within the agent's policy. The team is choosing between two designs for messages like this: (A) escalate to a human whenever a sentiment model scores the message above 0.8 frustration; (B) acknowledge the frustration, offer to process the refund right away, and escalate only if the customer then repeats that they want a person. Which choice is best?
opcoes: Design B, because the duplicate charge is within the agent's authority, so fixing it now and acknowledging the frustration avoids using a human slot.
Design A, because a customer who complains about a repeated mistake is likely to ask for a manager anyway, so an early handoff avoids a second bad interaction.
A combination: issue the refund first and then hand the case to a human, so that a person can follow up on the complaint about recurring billing mistakes.
Design A with the threshold raised to 0.95, so that only the most frustrated customers reach a human while the milder complaints stay with the agent.
questoes.explicacao: Frustration alone is not an escalation trigger when the issue is straightforward and within the agent's capability. The agent should acknowledge the frustration, offer the resolution, and escalate only if the customer reiterates that they want a human. Sentiment scores are an unreliable proxy for case complexity, whatever threshold is used.
feedbacks: Correct. Acknowledge the frustration, offer the in-policy refund, and escalate only if the customer repeats a preference for a person.
Sentiment does not measure complexity; escalating a simple, in-policy refund lowers first-contact resolution and makes the customer wait for something the agent can do now.
Sending every resolved-but-annoyed customer to a human spends human capacity on cases with no open question; fixing the charge resolves the complaint.
A higher threshold still escalates on sentiment instead of on the real triggers: an explicit request, a policy gap, or inability to make progress.

questoes.pergunta: Halden & Pierce's support agent handles long scheduling-and-billing conversations (often 35+ turns) and condenses older turns with progressive summarization to stay within its context budget. After summarization, the agent offered to move "your May session" when the customer had two (ENG-3317 on May 14 and ENG-3342 on May 21), and it forgot that the customer had said only 3 of their 10 prepaid hours remained. The requirement is that order numbers, dates, hour balances, statuses, and what the customer said they expect stay exact for the whole conversation. What should you change?
opcoes: Raise the summarization trigger from 60% to 85% of the context budget, so that older turns stay verbatim for longer before they are condensed into the summary.
Instruct the summarizer to copy every date, balance, and order number verbatim into its summaries, so that the condensed history keeps the exact details.
Call lookup_order and get_customer again at the start of every turn, so that the agent always works from fresh backend records instead of condensed history.
Keep a separate case facts block that is updated as facts emerge and sent with every prompt, so that these exact details never pass through the summarizer.
questoes.explicacao: Progressive summarization tends to blur exact identifiers, dates, balances, and customer expectations. Extracting transactional facts into a persistent case facts block, included in every prompt and kept outside the summarized history, preserves them however the conversation is condensed. The other options delay the loss, rely on the summarizer obeying, or flood the context with repeated tool output.
feedbacks: Only delays the problem: once the longer history is condensed, the same details get blurred, and the context budget fills sooner.
Tempting, but it still relies on a lossy summarization step to preserve every detail correctly, and it says nothing about what the customer expects.
Repeated lookups add verbose tool output that consumes context, and they cannot recover what the customer said, such as the hour balance they reported.
Correct. A case facts block kept outside the summarized history keeps transactional facts exact in every turn.

questoes.pergunta: At Halden & Pierce, policy says that process_refund may be called only after get_customer returns verification_level: "strong", meaning the customer passed a one-time code check. The system prompt states this rule in its own section, in capital letters, with two examples. A monthly audit finds 41 of 6,200 refunds issued to customers whose verification_level was "basic", and rewording the rule in March and again in April did not change the rate. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The rule sits in the middle of a long system prompt, so position effects make the model overlook it; moving the section to the top would close the gap.
The two examples cover only routine cases, so the model does not generalize the rule to unusual requests; more varied few-shot examples would close the gap.
Ordering that lives only in instructions keeps a small residual miss rate, and a refund that must never skip verification needs a check the model cannot bypass.
The values "strong" and "basic" are not explicit enough, so the model reads "basic" as sufficient; renaming them to "verified" and "unverified" would close the gap.
questoes.explicacao: A small, stable violation rate that survives repeated rewording is the signature of probabilistic compliance: prompt instructions, however emphatic, have a non-zero failure rate. When identity verification must precede a financial operation, the requirement is deterministic and calls for a programmatic prerequisite that blocks process_refund until verification_level is "strong". Prompt position, examples, and naming tweaks all remain probabilistic.
feedbacks: Lost-in-the-middle is real for long inputs, but two rewordings already failed to move the rate; any prompt-only change keeps a residual failure rate on a financial control.
More examples may shift the rate slightly, but they remain probabilistic guidance; a refund to an unverified customer needs a guarantee, not better odds.
Correct. Prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate; block process_refund in code until the prerequisite is met.
Clearer value names are harmless but do not change the nature of the control; the model can still skip or misapply a rule that only lives in the prompt.

questoes.pergunta: Halden & Pierce's support agent also has a resend_invoice tool that emails an invoice copy to an address passed as a parameter. The team is reviewing five rules that are currently written only in the system prompt and wants to move to Agent SDK hooks the ones where a single violation would be unacceptable, keeping the rest as prompt guidance. Which TWO rules should be enforced with hooks? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Refunds above $750 must always be routed to escalate_to_human instead of being processed by the agent.
A workshop credit should be offered before calling process_refund when the customer seems open to it.
resend_invoice must only send to the address on file that get_customer returned for the customer.
Replies must acknowledge the customer's concern before sharing what get_customer or lookup_order returned.
Conversations must end with a recap of what process_refund or escalate_to_human did and what comes next.
questoes.explicacao: Hooks give deterministic guarantees, while prompt instructions give probabilistic compliance. The refund threshold and the invoice destination are business and data-protection rules where one violation causes financial loss or a data leak, so a hook should intercept process_refund or resend_invoice calls and block or redirect them. Tone, offering alternatives, and recaps are judgment or style guidance that fits the prompt.
feedbacks: Correct. A tool call interception hook can block process_refund above $750 and redirect the case to escalate_to_human.
Requires judgment about the customer's openness; it is guidance the model should weigh, not a rule to enforce mechanically.
Correct. A hook can compare the address argument with the verified email from get_customer and block any mismatch.
A style rule; occasional misses are tolerable, and a hook cannot judge whether a reply properly acknowledged the concern.
A communication practice best handled by the prompt; a missing recap is not the kind of failure that needs a guaranteed block.

questoes.pergunta: At Halden & Pierce, the billing MCP server returns lookup_order amounts as integer cents ("amount": 24000) and dates as Unix timestamps, while the CRM server returns dollars and ISO 8601 dates. After the agent quoted a $24,000 refund for a $240 seat, the team added a PostToolUse hook that converts lookup_order amounts to dollars and timestamps to ISO 8601. The wrong quotes stopped, but a teammate notices that the billing system's own logs still show cents and asks what the hook actually does. Which statement about the observed behavior is correct?
opcoes: The hook updates the values stored in the billing system, so the logs will show dollars once older records are converted by the same hook on their next lookup.
The hook runs after the model has read the raw result, so the fix works because the model re-reads the corrected values in its next turn and revises its figure.
The hook only helps because the system prompt also explains the cents format, so without that instruction the model would still misread the converted amounts.
The hook rewrites each lookup_order result on its way into the conversation, so the agent reasons over converted values while the source data is left untouched.
questoes.explicacao: A PostToolUse hook intercepts the tool result after the tool runs and before the model processes it, so it can normalize heterogeneous formats such as cents, Unix timestamps, and status codes. The source system is untouched; only what enters the conversation changes. That is why the logs still show cents while the agent now quotes correct amounts.
feedbacks: The hook transforms the result on its way to the model; it does not write back to the billing system, so stored data and logs keep their original format.
Wrong timing: the point of a PostToolUse transformation is that the model never sees the raw value, so there is nothing to re-read or revise.
The converted values are already in dollars and ISO 8601; the hook makes the prompt explanation unnecessary rather than depending on it.
Correct. The hook normalizes the tool result before the model processes it, leaving the backend unchanged.

questoes.pergunta: In Halden & Pierce's support agent, the coordinator first runs an order-history subagent and a policy subagent, then asks a drafting subagent to write the resolution. The drafting subagent's prompt currently reads: "Draft a resolution for customer C-4471's dispute; the other subagents already checked the orders and the policy." In about 1 of 5 cases the draft cites a wrong amount or invents a policy term. An engineer proposes giving the drafting subagent lookup_order and a policy lookup tool so it can check both itself. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Accept it, because letting the drafting subagent query the backend itself ensures it works from current records rather than from findings produced earlier.
Reject it, and put the full order-history results and policy excerpts from the other two subagents into the drafting prompt, so that it drafts from them.
Reject it, and let the drafting subagent read the coordinator's conversation history, so that it sees the earlier subagents' outputs where they were returned.
Accept it, but limit the drafting subagent to read-only tools, so that its extra lookups cannot change the state of any order or refund along the way.
questoes.explicacao: The drafting subagent invents details because it receives none of the earlier findings; subagents only know what their prompt contains. The fix is to pass the complete results of the order-history and policy subagents directly in its prompt. Giving it lookup tools duplicates work, adds latency, and spreads tools outside its specialization.
feedbacks: Re-querying repeats work that already succeeded, adds latency, and gives the drafting subagent tools outside its role, which invites misuse.
Correct. Pass the prior agents' complete findings directly in the subagent's prompt so the draft is grounded in them.
Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's history; there is no shared conversation to read, so the findings must be passed in the prompt.
Read-only access reduces risk but keeps the duplication and the cross-role tooling; the real gap is that the findings are not passed along.

questoes.pergunta: Halden & Pierce's support agent uses two MCP servers owned by different teams: billing (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund) and scheduling (find_session, reschedule_session). An engineer wrote a router that first asks the model which server a request needs and then connects the agent only to that server, which adds about 1.8 seconds per request and fails on mixed requests such as "refund my seat and move my next session." The two servers must stay separate. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Merge the scheduling tools into the billing MCP server, so that the agent connects to a single server and every tool is reachable in one connection.
Keep the router but let it pick both servers when a request mentions both topics, so that mixed requests reconnect once with all the tools they need.
Configure both servers for the agent at startup, so that their tools are discovered on connection and the model can call any of them within a request.
Keep the router and cache each server connection after its first use, so that switching between the two servers no longer adds latency to each request.
questoes.explicacao: Tools from all configured MCP servers are discovered when the agent connects and are available at the same time, so there is no need to pick a server per request. Configuring both servers lets the model choose tools from either one within the same conversation, which also handles mixed requests. Merging violates the ownership constraint, and router variants keep an unnecessary, brittle step.
feedbacks: Would work technically but violates the requirement to keep the servers separate, and it is unnecessary because several servers can be active at once.
Still adds a pre-classification step that can misjudge requests, and reconnecting per request is unnecessary when both servers can stay connected.
Correct. Configured MCP servers are discovered together and their tools are available simultaneously, so the router can be removed.
Addresses latency only; the router still has to guess one server and still breaks requests that need tools from both.

questoes.pergunta: Halden & Pierce's support agent can use the built-in Grep and Read tools on a local folder of reply templates and past policy drafts, and an MCP tool, search_policy, whose description is "Searches policies." search_policy returns the clause currently in force, with its effective date and regional exceptions. Logs show that for 64% of policy questions the agent greps the local folder instead and sometimes quotes an outdated refund window. Grep is still needed for the reply templates. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Remove Grep from the agent's tools, so that search_policy becomes the only way the agent can look up policy wording during a conversation.
Add a system prompt rule that policy questions must go to search_policy, so that the agent stops grepping the local folder for refund terms.
Delete the superseded drafts from the local folder, so that a Grep search over policy text can only return clauses that are still in force.
Expand the MCP tool's description to explain what it returns and why that beats the local files, so that the model has a reason to choose it.
questoes.explicacao: The agent prefers Grep because the MCP tool's one-line description gives no reason to choose it. Expanding the description to explain what search_policy returns (the current clause, effective dates, regional exceptions) lets the model pick the more capable tool. Removing Grep breaks the template workflow, a keyword rule in the system prompt is a weaker substitute, and cleaning the folder still leaves the agent without regional exceptions.
feedbacks: Too blunt: Grep is still needed for reply templates, and removing it treats the symptom instead of making search_policy's value clear.
A prompt rule may help, but the root cause is a description that does not explain the tool's capabilities; fix that first.
Useful housekeeping, but the local files still lack effective dates and regional exceptions, so the agent keeps choosing a weaker source.
Correct. Detailed MCP tool descriptions stop the agent from defaulting to built-in tools like Grep when the MCP tool is more capable.

questoes.pergunta: In Halden & Pierce's support agent, a customer's first message is: "Please put me through to a person. It's about my last invoice." The customer is calm and has said nothing else. The team is choosing between two designs: (A) the agent first calls get_customer and lookup_order to try to resolve the invoice question, and offers a human only if that fails; (B) the agent escalates right away with escalate_to_human, passing along what the customer said. Which choice is best?
opcoes: Design A, because a quick lookup often resolves invoice questions, so trying first raises first-contact resolution while still offering a human afterward.
Design A, limited to a single lookup_order call, so that the delay stays short and the human receives a pre-investigated case if escalation follows.
Design B, but only after the agent explains what it can do and the customer repeats the request, so that avoidable escalations are filtered out.
Design B, because the request for a person was stated plainly, so the handoff should happen now, with the reason the customer gave attached to it.
questoes.explicacao: An explicit request for a human is an escalation trigger that should be honored immediately, without first attempting investigation. Trying to resolve first, even briefly, overrides the customer's stated preference. Offering resolution and waiting for the customer to repeat the request applies to frustrated customers with straightforward issues, not to explicit requests.
feedbacks: Raising first-contact resolution does not justify overriding an explicit request for a person; the agent should honor it right away.
Even a short investigation delays an explicit request; the handoff should happen first, with whatever context is already available.
Confuses two patterns: waiting for a repeated request fits a frustrated customer with a simple issue, not one who already asked for a person.
Correct. Explicit requests for a human are honored immediately, without trying to resolve the issue first.

questoes.pergunta: At Halden & Pierce, process_refund currently returns {"isError": true, "content": "Refund failed"} for every failure. Logs show the agent retrying three times when a refund is outside the 90-day policy window, telling customers to wait when the payment gateway timed out once, and escalating malformed amounts it could have corrected. The requirement is that the agent retries only failures that can succeed on retry, explains policy violations to the customer, fixes bad input, and escalates when it lacks authorization. What should you change?
opcoes: Put a short numeric code in the error text, such as E401 or E422, so that the agent can look up each code in a table included in its system prompt.
Make process_refund retry internally three times on a failure, so that only persistent failures reach the agent as one consolidated error message.
Return a category for every failure (transient, validation, business, or permission) and an isRetryable flag, so that the agent knows what to do.
Have the agent call escalate_to_human whenever a refund fails, so that a person decides how to handle each failure instead of the agent guessing.
questoes.explicacao: A uniform "Refund failed" hides the information the agent needs to choose a recovery. Classifying failures as transient (retry), validation (fix the input), business (explain the policy, not retryable), or permission (escalate), with an isRetryable flag and a readable description, lets the agent act correctly in each case. Internal retries and blanket escalation treat all failures the same way.
feedbacks: Codes help a little, but they push classification into a prompt lookup table; structured fields such as errorCategory and isRetryable are clearer and less error-prone.
Retrying a policy violation or a malformed amount wastes attempts; the problem is that failure types are not distinguished, not how many retries happen.
Correct. Structured error categories let the agent retry transient errors, fix validation errors, explain business errors, and escalate permission errors.
Pushes every failure to humans, including timeouts and fixable input errors, which lowers first-contact resolution without adding information.

questoes.pergunta: In Halden & Pierce's support agent, a customer writes in one message: "My March invoice charged 12 hours but I used 9, my April workshop seat was cancelled without a refund, and I can't log in to the portal." The agent resolved the March hours thoroughly and closed the conversation without addressing the seat or the login. Across conversations that raise several issues, 23% end with at least one issue unaddressed. Logs show the agent starts calling tools for the first issue immediately after reading the message. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The agent does not first break the message into separate items, so it works on whichever issue comes first and wraps up once that thread is resolved.
The conversation history grows long while the first issue is investigated, so the later concerns end up in the middle of the context and get overlooked.
The agent lacks a dedicated tool for portal login problems, so it cannot investigate that concern and drops it from the reply without saying so.
The system prompt asks for concise replies, so the agent leaves out secondary concerns to keep its final message short and focused on one issue.
questoes.explicacao: The pattern (tools called for the first issue right away, other issues dropped, including a seat refund that existing tools can handle) shows that the agent never decomposes multi-concern requests. It should break the message into distinct items, investigate each, in parallel where possible and with shared context, and then synthesize one resolution that covers all of them.
feedbacks: Correct. Multi-concern requests should be decomposed into distinct items, investigated, and synthesized into one unified resolution.
Position effects matter in long inputs, but these issues sit together in the first message; the agent never planned to address them.
Could explain the login issue, but not the seat refund, which lookup_order and process_refund can handle; the omission is broader than a missing tool.
Concise wording affects length, not scope; even a short reply could cover all three issues if the agent had identified them.

questoes.pergunta: At Halden & Pierce, an engineer wrote the support agent's loop so that it ends the turn whenever a response contains a text block longer than 40 characters, on the theory that the agent only writes to the customer once it is done. In 7% of conversations the customer receives "Let me pull up your recent orders and check that charge." and nothing more: the same response contained a lookup_order tool_use block that was never executed. What is the flaw in this implementation?
opcoes: The 40-character threshold is too low; raising it to 150 characters would make the loop wait until the agent has written a complete answer for the customer.
Completion is inferred from the presence of text; stop_reason, which says whether the model asked for a tool, is what should decide whether to continue.
Text-length checks are too crude; a small classifier that labels each reply as final or not final would detect completion far more reliably.
The model mixes customer text and tool calls in one response; instructing it to call tools silently would keep lookup_order from being skipped.
questoes.explicacao: The loop treats assistant text as a completion signal, which is an anti-pattern: Claude often writes text alongside a tool_use block. The response that announced the lookup had stop_reason "tool_use", so the loop should have executed lookup_order, appended the result, and continued; it should end only on "end_turn". Tuning thresholds or classifying text keeps the same flawed signal.
feedbacks: A higher threshold is still a text-based completion check; a longer interim message with a tool call would be cut off the same way.
Correct. Loop control should follow stop_reason ("tool_use" continues, "end_turn" stops), not the presence or length of text.
A classifier is a more elaborate way to parse natural language; stop_reason already states whether the model wants a tool run.
Text alongside tool calls is normal and expected; changing the model's output style works around the bug instead of fixing the loop.

questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The planning office of Lakeshore Regional Transit, a municipal transit agency, uses a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK to prepare cited reports for its board. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates the final report. While scoping a request, the coordinator itself called fetch_pdf on the agency's 40-page draft Network Plan, and the full text came back into the coordinator's conversation. It then invoked the document analysis subagent with the prompt "Analyze the ridership targets in the plan we just loaded." The subagent replied that no plan was provided and, on a retry, produced targets that appear nowhere in the document. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: The subagent received the plan but lost it among other content, because long tool results that arrive early in a conversation carry less weight later on.
The plan was too long to share, so the coordinator should have split it into pages and called the subagent once per page with the same short prompt.
Subagents can see the coordinator's tool results, but only results the coordinator marks as shared context are carried into a delegated task.
The subagent saw only its own prompt, so the plan's text, or a reference it can load itself, has to be written into the delegation explicitly.
questoes.explicacao: Subagents operate with isolated context: they do not inherit the coordinator's conversation history, including tool results the coordinator received. "The plan we just loaded" points at something the subagent never saw, so it either reports nothing or invents content. The coordinator must pass the relevant text, or a document reference plus the means to load it, explicitly in the Task prompt.
feedbacks: Assumes the subagent received the plan; it did not, because the coordinator's tool results are not part of its context.
Splitting does not help while the prompt still refers to a plan the subagent cannot see; the content itself has to be passed.
There is no shared-context marking that exposes the coordinator's history; subagents start with only what their prompt provides.
Correct. Subagent context is isolated from the coordinator's history, so the plan must be passed explicitly in the Task prompt.

questoes.pergunta: In Lakeshore Transit's research system, the document analysis subagent runs its own loop on the Messages API. To bound latency, an engineer proposes this design: if the first response has stop_reason "tool_use", run the requested tools, append the results, make exactly one more request, and take that second response as the final analysis. Typical analyses fetch a PDF, extract its tables, and then check key figures against a second source. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Reject it: a later response can also have stop_reason "tool_use", so tools must keep running and results keep returning until "end_turn".
Accept it, because Claude requests every tool it needs in its first response, so one round of tool results is enough to complete each analysis.
Accept it, but if the second response still asks for tools, run them and attach their outputs to the final answer without making another request.
Reject it, and instead keep looping until the response text says the analysis is complete, since that wording shows Claude is done with the tools.
questoes.explicacao: In the agentic loop, each response is inspected: stop_reason "tool_use" means the code must execute the requested tools, append the results to the conversation, and send the next request; "end_turn" means Claude is done. Multi-step analyses (fetch, then extract, then verify) need as many iterations as the model requests, so a fixed two-request design truncates them. Ending on text wording is a different anti-pattern.
feedbacks: Correct. Keep iterating while stop_reason is "tool_use", returning results each time, and stop on "end_turn".
Claude chooses the next tool based on earlier results; tables can only be extracted after the PDF has been fetched.
Running tools without returning their results to Claude skips the reasoning step; raw outputs are not an analysis.
Parsing natural-language signals to decide termination is an anti-pattern; stop_reason states whether Claude is done.

questoes.pergunta: In Lakeshore Transit's research system, analysts spent a two-hour session building a baseline analysis of ridership data and 30 sources on bus network redesign. The board now wants two report variants, one assuming a frequency-first network and one assuming a coverage-first network. The analysts kept working in the same session: after the frequency-first variant was drafted, the coverage-first draft kept borrowing its assumptions. Rebuilding the baseline would take another two hours. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Start two new sessions and paste a short summary of the baseline into each, so that both variants begin clean without carrying the other's assumptions.
Branch twice from the point where the baseline was finished, so that each variant inherits that analysis and neither sees the other's draft.
Stay in the same session and tell Claude to disregard the frequency-first draft, so that the coverage-first variant builds only on the baseline.
Resume the baseline session twice in parallel with --resume, so that both variants share the baseline and can see each other's progress as they go.
questoes.explicacao: fork_session creates independent branches from a shared baseline, which is exactly what two divergent variants need: both inherit the full two-hour analysis, and neither sees the other's work. A short summary loses baseline detail that is still valid, and asking the model to disregard earlier content in the same session does not remove it from context.
feedbacks: A fresh start with a summary fits when earlier tool results are stale; here the baseline is valid, and a short summary discards detail that took two hours to build.
Correct. fork_session from the shared baseline gives each variant the full analysis without cross-contamination.
The frequency-first draft stays in the context window; an instruction to ignore it does not reliably stop it from influencing the second draft.
Sharing progress between variants is the problem being solved; the variants need isolated branches, not a shared view of each other's work.

questoes.pergunta: In Lakeshore Transit's research system, the document analysis subagent pulls datasets from the state's open-data portal, whose API times out on about 6% of calls; nearly all of them succeed when retried a few seconds later. Today every timeout is passed straight to the coordinator, which re-plans and re-delegates the whole analysis task, adding 4 to 7 minutes per report. Occasionally a dataset has been moved behind a login and returns 403. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Have the coordinator retry the whole analysis task automatically on a subagent error, so that transient timeouts are absorbed without the coordinator re-planning.
Have the subagent skip datasets that fail to load and report success for the rest, so that the coordinator is not interrupted by these fetch errors.
Mirror the open-data portal into the agency's own storage every night, so that the subagent no longer depends on the external API during analysis.
Have the subagent retry timeouts itself and pass up only what it cannot fix, such as a 403, with what it tried and found, so that the coordinator re-plans less.
questoes.explicacao: Transient failures should be recovered locally by the subagent; only errors it cannot resolve go to the coordinator, together with what was attempted and the partial results. That removes the costly re-planning for timeouts while still surfacing a dataset that now needs access, so the coordinator can look for an alternative. Whole-task retries, silent skipping, and infrastructure mirroring each miss part of this.
feedbacks: Still restarts the entire analysis for a failure that a single quick retry would fix, keeping most of the added minutes.
Silently suppresses failures: the coordinator would believe the analysis is complete, and the report could miss key datasets.
Heavy infrastructure for a problem that local retries solve; it is not a proportionate first step and adds a sync process to maintain.
Correct. Recover transient errors locally and propagate only unresolved ones, with what was attempted and the partial results.

questoes.pergunta: In Lakeshore Transit's research system, the agency's ridership MCP server exposes query_ridership. When something goes wrong, the tool returns an ordinary result whose text starts with "Error:", for example "Error: end date before start date" or "Error: warehouse unavailable". In 9 of 120 reports last quarter, the analysis subagent quoted these strings as findings, such as ridership being "unavailable" on a route. The team is choosing between two designs: (A) keep failures as ordinary results and add a prompt instruction to watch for the "Error:" prefix; (B) return failures with the MCP isError flag set and a description of what went wrong. Which choice is best?
opcoes: Design A, because a consistent text prefix is easy for the model to recognize, and the prompt instruction makes the meaning of that prefix explicit.
Design B, because the flag tells the agent at the protocol level that the call failed, so the text is read as a problem to handle rather than as data.
Design A with JSON content such as {"status": "error"}, because a structured body is parsed more reliably than a text prefix inside a normal result.
Design B for warehouse outages only, because an invalid date range is the agent's own mistake and should come back as a normal result with a hint.
questoes.explicacao: The MCP isError flag is the standard way to tell the agent that a tool call failed, so the content is read as an error description rather than as a result. Returning errors as normal content, even with a prefix or a JSON status, relies on the model noticing a convention. Validation errors such as an invalid date range are failures too, and flagging them lets the agent correct the input.
feedbacks: Relies on the model consistently noticing a prefix inside successful results, which is exactly what failed in 9 reports.
Correct. The isError flag communicates failure through the protocol so the agent can choose a recovery.
Structured content helps the model read the error, but the call is still marked as a success, so the failure signal remains a convention.
An invalid input is a validation error, not a successful result; flagging it lets the agent fix the date range and retry.

questoes.pergunta: In Lakeshore Transit's research system, two credible sources give different 2023 farebox recovery ratios for a peer agency: its audited annual report says 18.4%, and a federal transit database profile says 21.1% for the same fiscal year. The document analysis subagent currently keeps the value from the source it judges more authoritative and drops the other. The board now requires reports to show where credible sources disagree. What should you change?
opcoes: Have the analysis subagent finish its output with both figures, each tied to its source and annotated as a disagreement, so that the coordinator decides.
Have the analysis subagent stop and return an error when sources disagree, so that the coordinator can send the question back to search for a third source.
Have the analysis subagent report the average of the two values with both sources cited, so that the synthesis subagent receives one figure it can use.
Have the synthesis subagent compare the sources for disagreements at the end, so that conflicts are resolved in one place with the findings in view.
questoes.explicacao: The analysis subagent should complete its work with conflicting values kept and explicitly annotated with their sources, and leave reconciliation to the coordinator before synthesis. Picking one value, averaging, or aborting each loses information or progress. Moving conflict detection to synthesis is too late, because the analysis step has already discarded one of the values.
feedbacks: Correct. Keep both values with attribution and a conflict annotation, and let the coordinator decide before synthesis.
Stopping on a conflict throws away completed analysis; a third source may help, but that is the coordinator's call once it sees both values.
Averaging invents a number neither source reported and hides the disagreement the board asked to see.
By the time synthesis runs, the analysis step has already dropped one value, so there is no conflict left to detect.

questoes.pergunta: In Lakeshore Transit's research system, the document analysis subagent receives 16 sets of board-meeting minutes (2019–2024) in one request and is asked to list every service change and how the changes relate. Its summary says route 12 was "cut in 2020 and never restored" while quoting the 2023 restoration a few paragraphs later, lists the 2021 fare change twice with different effective dates, and covers the 2022 meetings in one line each. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The 16 documents exceed what the subagent can attend to in one request, so a model with a larger context window would give each meeting adequate coverage.
Local extraction and cross-meeting reasoning happen in one combined step, instead of a step per document followed by a separate step that relates them.
The prompt does not define what counts as a service change, so the subagent applies a different threshold to each meeting and misses related changes.
The web search subagent passed too many documents at once, and it should have filtered the set down to the five most relevant before delegating.
questoes.explicacao: Self-contradictions about the same change, duplicated items, and uneven coverage are signs of attention dilution in a single pass. Prompt chaining fixes it: analyze each document on its own for local facts, then run a separate cross-document pass that relates the changes. A larger context window does not fix attention quality, and dropping documents loses coverage.
feedbacks: A bigger context window does not solve attention dilution; the model can hold all 16 documents and still treat them unevenly.
Correct. Chain the work: per-document analysis first, then a dedicated integration pass across documents.
A definition of "service change" would not explain the self-contradiction or the duplicate entry, which come from doing everything at once.
Every meeting is needed to trace changes over time; cutting to five documents would remove exactly the history the question asks about.

questoes.pergunta: In Lakeshore Transit's research system, the analysis subagent returns each finding as {"claim", "value", "source_url", "excerpt"}. A recent report stated that "sources disagree on route 9 daily ridership: 4,100 versus 6,800," and the board asked which figure was wrong. Both were accurate: one came from a 2019 manual count and the other from a 2024 automatic passenger counter dataset. What is the flaw in this implementation?
opcoes: The schema lacks a confidence score for each claim, so the synthesis subagent cannot tell which of the two ridership values is the more reliable one.
The excerpt field is too short to carry context, so the synthesis subagent cannot see the surrounding methodology that would explain the difference.
The synthesis subagent is told to flag disagreements, so it reports a conflict instead of keeping the value from the more authoritative of the two.
Nothing in each finding says when the figure was published or measured, so a real change between two years is presented as two sources disagreeing.
questoes.explicacao: Without publication or collection dates in the structured output, a change over time looks like a contradiction. Requiring subagents to include those dates lets the synthesis subagent interpret the two figures correctly as 2019 and 2024 values. Confidence scores, longer excerpts, or picking one source do not supply the missing temporal information.
feedbacks: Both figures were accurate, so reliability is not the issue; what was missing is when each was measured.
Longer excerpts might happen to include a date, but relying on that is fragile; the date should be a required structured field.
Flagging genuine conflicts is correct behavior; the problem is that this was not a conflict, and the schema gave no way to tell.
Correct. Requiring publication or collection dates in structured outputs prevents temporal differences from being read as contradictions.

questoes.pergunta: Lakeshore Transit's board asks the research system for "a comprehensive report on everything that affects on-time performance across our bus network." The coordinator told the web search subagent to collect everything it could find; three hours later it had gathered about 900 sources, the analysis subagent had worked through them in arrival order, and the draft still says nothing about operator shortages, which planners know are a major cause. Which TWO changes to the coordinator's approach would best address this? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Cap the search at the 100 most relevant sources and analyze them in parallel, so that the coordinator receives a manageable set of findings much sooner.
Split the topic into a fixed list of ten standard delay causes from a transit textbook, so that each search covers one cause and coverage is complete from the start.
Rank areas by likely effect on delays and revise the plan as findings reveal links, so that a shortage touching many routes gets its own line of inquiry.
Ask the synthesis subagent to infer missing causes from the sources already gathered, so that gaps such as staffing are covered without new searches.
Start by mapping the data sources, delay categories, and route groupings, so that the research tasks follow how the problem is actually organized.
questoes.explicacao: Open-ended tasks should be decomposed by first mapping the structure of the problem, then identifying high-impact areas and building a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered. Collecting everything and processing it in arrival order produces volume without coverage of the causes that matter most. A fixed textbook list, a source cap, or inference at synthesis time do not change the decomposition.
feedbacks: Capping and parallelizing speeds things up but still has no structure or priorities; the most important causes can fall outside the first 100 sources.
A fixed list ignores what Lakeshore's own data shows and cannot adapt when new dependencies appear.
Correct. Prioritizing high-impact areas and adapting as dependencies emerge keeps the plan focused and complete.
Synthesis can only combine what was found; if no search investigated staffing, there is no evidence to infer it from.
Correct. Mapping the structure first lets the coordinator create subtasks that reflect the real problem space.

questoes.pergunta: In Lakeshore Transit's research system, a board analyst asks the coordinator to track four inquiries in one working session: INQ-1 (route 22 crowding), INQ-2 (paratransit wait times), INQ-3 (fare evasion estimates), and INQ-4 (bike lane conflicts). After about 50 turns, the coordinator attributes INQ-2's 38-minute average wait to INQ-1 and reports INQ-3 as complete although it is still waiting for a source. An engineer proposes summarizing all four inquiries into one running narrative every 10 turns. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Accept it, because a regular narrative summary keeps the coordinator's context small enough that the four inquiries stop interfering with one another.
Accept it, but write each inquiry's summary as its own paragraph, so that the narrative keeps the figures of different inquiries visually separated.
Reject it, and split the work into four independent coordinator sessions, so that each inquiry is handled with no shared context between them.
Reject it, and hold each inquiry's ID, figures, and status as a structured record outside the summarized history, so that each turn has exact values.
questoes.explicacao: In multi-issue sessions, structured issue data such as IDs, figures, and statuses should be extracted into a separate context layer that is included in every prompt. Narrative summaries, even organized by paragraph, are where figures get blurred and statuses drift. Splitting into four sessions loses the shared context the analyst relies on, such as overlaps between inquiries.
feedbacks: Summarization is what blurs figures and statuses; repeating it every 10 turns adds more chances to mix up inquiries.
Better organized, but still a lossy narrative rewritten by the model, so figures and statuses can drift between rewrites.
Overcorrects: the analyst loses a single working session and any cross-inquiry context, and each session can still drift internally.
Correct. Persist structured per-inquiry data in a separate context layer so IDs, figures, and statuses stay exact.

questoes.pergunta: Lakeshore Transit's research system runs the same fixed pipeline for every request: search, analyze, synthesize, report. For routine monthly ridership briefs this works well. For the question "Why did weekend ridership on the east corridor drop 22% in Q2?", the first search found that the drop coincided with a bridge-closure detour, but the pipeline continued with its generic demographic analysis and never examined the detour. The team wants to keep the routine briefs unchanged. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Add a sixth fixed step that reviews detours and construction for every request, so that the pipeline covers the cause found in this case from now on.
Replace the fixed pipeline with adaptive planning for every request, so that the routine monthly briefs also benefit from findings-driven subtasks.
For open-ended "why" questions, let the coordinator add subtasks based on what each step turns up, so that the monthly briefs keep the fixed chain.
Keep the fixed pipeline but give the synthesis subagent a web search tool, so that it can follow up on unexpected findings while writing the synthesis.
questoes.explicacao: Fixed prompt chains suit predictable, repeatable work like the monthly briefs, while open-ended investigations need adaptive plans that generate subtasks from intermediate findings. Here the detour finding should have produced new subtasks, such as comparing ridership on detoured trips. Adding a fixed step only covers this one cause, and changing the routine briefs violates the constraint.
feedbacks: Patches the last incident: the next investigation will hinge on a different cause that no fixed step anticipates.
The routine briefs work well with a fixed chain; switching them adds variability and cost the team explicitly wants to avoid.
Correct. Use adaptive investigation plans where findings should drive the next subtasks, and prompt chaining where the work is predictable.
Gives the synthesis agent a tool outside its specialization, and the plan itself still would not adapt to what was discovered.

questoes.pergunta: In Lakeshore Transit's research system, the coordinator always invokes the same three subagents (web search, synthesis, report), whatever the request. When board members attach their own documents, such as a 300-page consultant study, and ask how its recommendations compare with peer agencies, the report ignores the attachment, because the document analysis subagent is never called. Simple web questions are handled well. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Train a separate classifier to label each request by type before the coordinator runs, so that requests with attachments go to a different pipeline.
Have the coordinator examine what each request contains and needs and invoke the subagents that fit, so that attachments reach the analysis subagent.
Make the coordinator invoke all four subagents on every request, so that attached documents are always analyzed even when a request does not need it.
Give the synthesis subagent a tool to read attachments directly, so that it can fold the consultant study into the comparison while it writes.
questoes.explicacao: Deciding which subagents to invoke based on what a query requires is part of the coordinator's role. A coordinator that analyzes each request (attachments, scope, complexity) and selects subagents dynamically would send the consultant study to the document analysis subagent and keep simple questions light. A separate classifier is heavier than adjusting the coordinator, always running every subagent wastes work on simple requests, and giving synthesis a reading tool spreads tools outside its role.
feedbacks: Over-engineered as a first step: it adds labeled data and infrastructure for a decision the coordinator can make itself.
Correct. The coordinator should analyze each request and select subagents dynamically instead of always running the same fixed set.
Fixes this case by always running the full pipeline, which wastes time and cost on the simple questions that work well today.
Gives the synthesis subagent a tool outside its specialization; document analysis already exists and should simply be invoked.

questoes.pergunta: In Lakeshore Transit's research system, the web search subagent's regional studies tool returns an error both when the studies database times out and when a query runs successfully but matches nothing. As a result, the coordinator retries queries that simply have no matches, adding about 9 minutes per report, and reports say "source unavailable" for topics where no local study exists. Which TWO changes should you make? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Have the tool return an empty list for every failure as well, so that the coordinator stops retrying and the reports simply move on to other topics.
Have the tool return an empty success only when the query really ran and matched nothing, so that "none found" can be stated as a finding.
Have the report subagent write "no studies found" wherever a search failed, so that readers are not told that sources were down when they were not.
Have the coordinator stop retrying failed searches after the first attempt, so that queries with no matches no longer add minutes to each report.
Have the tool report a timeout as a failed call with the error type and the query it attempted, so the subagent can choose to retry or switch sources.
questoes.explicacao: Access failures and valid empty results mean different things: a timeout needs a retry or alternative decision, while a successful query with no matches is a real finding that should not be retried. The tool must distinguish them, reporting the timeout as a failure with context and returning an empty success only when the query actually ran. Blanket retry limits, rewording reports, or turning all failures into empty lists each blur the distinction.
feedbacks: Silently suppresses real failures as empty successes, so timeouts would be reported as if no studies existed.
Correct. A valid empty result should be returned as success so it is not retried and can be reported as a real finding.
Masks real outages as findings; when the database actually timed out, "no studies found" would be false.
Stops retries for real timeouts too; the tool still cannot tell the coordinator which failures are worth retrying.
Correct. An access failure should be reported as a failure with context so the agent can make a retry decision.

questoes.pergunta: In Lakeshore Transit's research system, the report generation subagent runs a loop with a fixed five iterations. For short reports, Claude finishes at iteration 2 and the code keeps sending "continue" messages, which produces duplicated sections; for long reports, the loop stops at iteration 5 while Claude is still requesting chart and citation tools. The requirement is that the subagent keeps running tools as long as Claude needs them and stops exactly when Claude is done. What should you change?
opcoes: Loop while stop_reason is "tool_use" and exit on "end_turn", so that the number of iterations follows what Claude actually requests.
Keep the five iterations but exit early once the report contains a heading named "References", so that finished reports are not extended further.
Raise the loop to ten iterations and remove repeated sections afterward, so that long reports can finish and short ones are cleaned up automatically.
Exit as soon as a response has no tool_use blocks or contains a text block, so that the subagent stops once Claude starts writing its prose.
questoes.explicacao: The loop should be driven by stop_reason: continue while it is "tool_use", executing the tools and appending their results, and terminate when it is "end_turn". This runs exactly as many iterations as Claude needs. Fixed counts, content markers, and text detection are the patterns that cause both the duplicated and the truncated reports.
feedbacks: Correct. stop_reason tells the loop whether to execute tools and continue or to stop.
Uses report content as a completion signal, which breaks when a report has no references or the heading appears before the work is done.
A larger fixed cap still truncates some reports and wastes requests on others; post-processing hides the symptom.
Claude often writes text alongside tool calls, so stopping on any text block would cut off reports that still need tools.

questoes.pergunta: Lakeshore Transit's analysts continue a named research session, fare-study-2025, with --resume after a week away. In the meantime, the agency revised 2 of the 40 source documents the session had analyzed. The analysts opened with "Some sources may have changed; please make sure the analysis is current." The session then spent about 90 minutes re-reading and re-analyzing all 40 sources before producing anything new. What is the most likely root cause of the lost time?
opcoes: Resuming a session discards the earlier tool results, so --resume forces the session to rebuild its whole analysis from the original documents.
The session's context was nearly full after a week, so it could not find its earlier analysis and fell back to reading every source again.
The session was told only that something might have changed, not which files, so the only safe way to honor the request was to re-check everything.
The revised files kept their names, so the session could not tell them apart and had to invalidate its cached copies of all forty sources.
questoes.explicacao: A resumed session keeps its earlier analysis in the conversation history; what it needs is to be told which specific files changed so it can re-analyze only those. A vague "some sources may have changed" leaves it no way to target the work, so it re-explores everything. Naming the two revised documents would have limited the work to them.
feedbacks: --resume restores the prior conversation, including its tool results; nothing was discarded.
Nothing indicates a context problem; the session re-read the sources because the request gave it no way to know which ones changed.
Correct. Tell a resumed session which files changed so it re-analyzes them in a targeted way instead of re-exploring everything.
There is no cache of source copies to invalidate; the issue is that the session was not told which two documents were revised.

questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Vireo, a subscription video-on-demand service, has integrated Claude Code into the CI/CD pipeline of the monorepo behind its catalog, playback, and billing services. The pipeline runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and posts feedback on pull requests, and the team must design prompts that give actionable feedback while minimizing false positives. Vireo's root CLAUDE.md currently contains a 1,400-line release-notes procedure that is used once every two weeks, while the universal rule "never log subscriber email addresses" lives only in a /privacy-check skill that developers are expected to invoke. CI reviews miss email logging in about 30% of PRs that touch logging code. What is the flaw in this setup?
opcoes: The release-notes procedure should become a slash command in .claude/commands/, and developers should be reminded to run /privacy-check before opening a PR.
Both items belong in CLAUDE.md, but the file should be split with @import, so that the release-notes procedure is loaded from a separate, shorter file.
The two are placed backwards: the rule that applies to every change should be loaded in every session, and the biweekly procedure only when it is invoked.
Both items belong in skills, but /privacy-check should set context: fork, so that its findings do not clutter the main review conversation in CI.
questoes.explicacao: CLAUDE.md is always loaded and is the place for universal standards that must apply in every session, including CI reviews. Skills are invoked on demand and suit task-specific workflows such as a biweekly release-notes procedure. Here the rule that must always apply depends on someone invoking a skill, while a rarely used procedure consumes context in every session.
feedbacks: Moving the procedure out is right, but leaving the privacy rule in a skill keeps it dependent on someone remembering to invoke it, so CI reviews still miss it.
@import only reorganizes the file; imported content is still loaded every time, and the privacy rule remains outside CLAUDE.md.
Correct. Universal standards belong in always-loaded CLAUDE.md; occasional workflows belong in on-demand skills.
context: fork isolates output but does not make the skill run automatically; the universal rule still depends on manual invocation.

questoes.pergunta: At Vireo, a platform engineer is turning a developer's local test-generation script into a CI step. Locally, running claude -p "Write unit tests for the files changed since main" printed the generated tests and returned to the shell. A colleague was surprised: they expected a chat session where they could ask follow-up questions, and they asked whether the flag also changes how project configuration is loaded. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: -p switches Claude Code to a reduced mode that skips CLAUDE.md and project settings, which is why it returns to the shell without asking any questions.
-p sends the prompt through the Message Batches API, which is why there is no live session and the result appears only once processing has completed.
-p is the non-interactive mode: the prompt is handled, the answer goes to standard output, and the process ends, with CLAUDE.md still providing context.
-p only hides the terminal interface, so a pipeline must still pipe an empty stdin to Claude Code to keep it from waiting for confirmation prompts.
questoes.explicacao: The -p (--print) flag runs Claude Code in non-interactive mode: it processes the prompt, prints the result to stdout, and exits, which is the expected behavior for automated pipelines. Project context such as CLAUDE.md still applies, which is how CI-invoked Claude Code receives testing standards and review criteria. The flag is unrelated to the Message Batches API.
feedbacks: Wrong: CLAUDE.md remains the mechanism for giving CI-invoked Claude Code its project context, such as testing standards.
Confuses the CLI flag with a different API; -p returns as soon as the prompt is processed, with no batch window.
Correct. -p is the documented non-interactive mode: process the prompt, print to stdout, exit.
Redirecting stdin is a workaround, not how Claude Code is run in pipelines; -p by itself prevents waiting for input.

questoes.pergunta: At Vireo, a PR triage service in the pipeline calls the Messages API directly with three tools: extract_pr_metadata (changed modules, linked ticket, risk area), lookup_code_owners, and fetch_test_history. The enrichment tools need the module list from extract_pr_metadata, but with tool_choice "auto" the model calls lookup_code_owners first, with guessed module names, in 11% of runs. A colleague proposes setting tool_choice to "any". How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Accept it, because "any" requires a tool call on the first turn, which is enough to make extract_pr_metadata run before the two enrichment tools.
Accept it, and add a system prompt line saying extract_pr_metadata must come first, so that the model picks it among the tools "any" allows.
Reject it: name extract_pr_metadata in a forced tool_choice for the first request, then let the enrichment calls happen in the turns that follow.
Reject it: keep "auto" but offer only extract_pr_metadata in the first request, and add the enrichment tools once the metadata has been returned.
questoes.explicacao: "any" guarantees that the model calls some tool, not which one, so lookup_code_owners could still come first. Forcing the specific tool with tool_choice {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_pr_metadata"} guarantees that the extraction runs first; the enrichment calls then happen in follow-up turns using its output. Offering a single tool under "auto" still lets the model answer in text instead of calling it.
feedbacks: "any" forces a tool call but lets the model choose among all the tools, so it does not guarantee the order.
Adds a probabilistic instruction on top of "any"; the ordering would still not be guaranteed.
Correct. Forced tool selection ({"type": "tool", "name": "extract_pr_metadata"}) guarantees that a specific tool runs first; later steps run in subsequent turns.
Close, but with "auto" the model may return text instead of calling the tool, so the first step is still not guaranteed.

questoes.pergunta: At Vireo, the root CLAUDE.md has grown to 2,900 lines covering Kotlin services, the TypeScript web player, Terraform, SQL migrations, and the Android app. Terraform modules and SQL migrations live inside each service's folder. On small PRs that touch only Terraform, the CI review spends most of its context on unrelated conventions and sometimes applies Kotlin naming rules to HCL files. The conventions must keep loading automatically, without anyone invoking them. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Split CLAUDE.md into area files and pull each one back in with @import, so that the root file stays short while the conventions remain available.
Turn each area's conventions into a skill, so that the review job loads only the conventions it explicitly invokes for the files in the PR.
Move each area into its own rule file whose glob matches that area's file types, so that a Terraform-only PR brings in only the Terraform conventions.
Place a CLAUDE.md in each top-level directory with that area's conventions, so that Claude reads only the file for the directory a PR touches.
questoes.explicacao: Path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ load only when Claude works with files matching their globs, which cuts irrelevant context and the cross-application of conventions. Because Terraform and SQL files are spread across service folders, globs such as **/*.tf work where directory-level CLAUDE.md files cannot. @import keeps everything loaded, and skills require invocation.
feedbacks: Modular, but imported files are still loaded in every session, so a Terraform-only PR still carries every convention.
Skills load on demand, which breaks the requirement that conventions apply automatically.
Correct. Path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ load only for matching files, reducing irrelevant context and token usage.
Directory-level files cannot follow Terraform and SQL files that live inside every service's folder.

questoes.pergunta: At Vireo, developers generate consumer contract tests by pasting a long procedure from the wiki into Claude Code. The team wants a reusable /gen-contract-tests workflow that is shared through the repository, runs in an isolated context so its verbose exploration does not fill the session, is limited to Read, Grep, Glob, and Write, and prompts for the service name when it is invoked without one. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Add the procedure to the root CLAUDE.md under a "Contract tests" heading, so that Claude follows it whenever a developer asks for contract tests.
Create .claude/skills/gen-contract-tests/SKILL.md with context: fork, allowed-tools, and argument-hint, so the repo carries the whole workflow.
Create ~/.claude/skills/gen-contract-tests/SKILL.md on each developer's machine, so that everyone can tailor the procedure to their services.
Define the workflow in .claude/settings.json under a skills entry with fork, tools, and argument fields, so that it is versioned with the repo.
questoes.explicacao: A project skill in .claude/skills/ with a SKILL.md is shared through version control, and its frontmatter supports exactly these requirements: context: fork for isolation, allowed-tools to restrict tools during the skill, and argument-hint to prompt for the service name. CLAUDE.md would load the procedure into every session, a personal skill is not shared, and settings.json has no such skills entry.
feedbacks: Always-loaded context for an occasional workflow, with no isolation, no tool restriction, and no argument prompt.
Correct. A project SKILL.md with context: fork, allowed-tools, and argument-hint meets every requirement.
Personal skills in ~/.claude/skills/ are not shared through the repository, so each developer's copy would drift.
Skills are not defined in settings.json; this configuration mechanism does not exist.

questoes.pergunta: At Vireo, the review criteria live in the tech lead's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, so CI reviews on ephemeral runners ignore them. The payments service also needs stricter rules for currency handling. The team is choosing between two designs: (A) bake the tech lead's user-level file, including the payment rules, into the CI runner image; (B) move the shared criteria into the project CLAUDE.md and add a directory-level CLAUDE.md in services/payments/ for the payment rules. Which choice is best?
opcoes: Design A, because a single file baked into the runner image ensures that every CI job loads the same criteria regardless of which files a PR touches.
Design B, because the repo's file reaches every developer and runner through version control, and the nested file adds the payment rules only where needed.
Design A, and also commit a copy of the file to the repo root, so that developers and CI runners load the same user-level criteria from version control.
Design B, but put the payment rules in each payments engineer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, so that only the engineers who work on payments load them.
questoes.explicacao: The CLAUDE.md hierarchy has user-level (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, personal and not shared), project-level (root or .claude/CLAUDE.md, versioned with the repo), and directory-level files for subdirectory-specific rules. Team review criteria belong at the project level, and payment-only rules fit a directory-level file in services/payments/. Baking a personal file into an image keeps the criteria outside version control and applies payment rules everywhere.
feedbacks: Works for CI only and keeps the team's criteria in one person's private file, outside version control; payment rules would also apply to every PR.
Correct. Project-level CLAUDE.md is shared through the repo, and a directory-level file scopes the payment rules.
A committed copy at the root is simply the project-level file; keeping a second, user-level master invites the two to drift apart.
User-level files are not shared and are not present on CI runners, so CI reviews of payments code would miss the rules.

questoes.pergunta: At Vireo, the nightly CI job generates tests for the playback service. Reviewers find that about 40% of generated tests only check getters, the tests build their own mock subscriber objects instead of using the existing fixtures in testing/fixtures/Subscribers.kt, and they use an assertion library the team does not use. The team wants every CI test-generation run to follow its standards, focus on valuable behavior, and use the existing fixtures. What should you change?
opcoes: Write down in the project CLAUDE.md how the team tests, which behaviors are worth covering, and which fixtures exist, so that each run starts with that context.
Add a post-generation filter that deletes tests whose names begin with "get" or "set", so that trivial getter tests never reach the pull request.
Include the full contents of every existing test file in each prompt, so that Claude infers the conventions and fixtures from the tests already there.
Ask reviewers to reject low-value tests in the PR and record the reasons, so that the job learns the team's standards from the review history over time.
questoes.explicacao: CLAUDE.md is how CI-invoked Claude Code receives project context. Documenting the testing standards, the criteria for a valuable test, and the available fixtures there improves every generation run and reduces low-value output. Name-based filters, inference from bulk test files, and reviewer rejections either treat symptoms or rely on context the job does not reliably get.
feedbacks: Correct. Testing standards, valuable-test criteria, and available fixtures documented in CLAUDE.md guide every CI test-generation run.
A name filter is a brittle heuristic; it misses trivial tests with other names and does nothing about fixtures or assertion style.
Sharing relevant existing tests helps avoid duplicates, but dumping every test file is costly, and inferred conventions are less reliable than documented ones.
Shifts the work to reviewers, and the CI job has no mechanism that learns from PR rejections.

questoes.pergunta: At Vireo, the review job's output is read by a script that posts inline PR comments. The prompt asks Claude to "respond with a JSON array of findings with file, line, severity, and message." In about 6% of runs the output has prose before the JSON or findings without a line field, and the posting step fails. Which TWO changes best make the output reliably machine-parseable? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Add a regex step that extracts the first JSON array from the output, so that prose before or after the findings no longer breaks parsing.
Run the job with --output-format json, so that the CLI returns a machine-readable result object that the posting script can parse directly.
Move the review to the Message Batches API, so that each result comes back as a JSON object keyed by custom_id for the posting script to read.
Pass the findings format to the CLI with --json-schema, so that a finding missing a field such as line cannot come back in the result.
Add few-shot examples of the JSON array to the review prompt, so that Claude reproduces the exact structure of the findings more often.
questoes.explicacao: --output-format json makes the CLI emit a machine-readable result, and --json-schema enforces the structure of the findings, including required fields. Together they produce structured findings that can be posted as inline PR comments without fragile parsing.
