Few-shot examples and regex extraction improve the odds without enforcing the structure, and the batch API is unsuitable for a review that gates PRs.
feedbacks: A regex hides prose but cannot add missing fields like line, and it breaks on nested or malformed output.
Correct. --output-format json gives the pipeline a machine-readable result instead of free text.
Batch processing has no latency guarantee, which does not fit PR feedback, and it does not by itself enforce the findings schema.
Correct. --json-schema enforces the findings' structure, including required fields.
Few-shot examples improve consistency but do not enforce it; the 6% of failures would shrink, not disappear.

questoes.pergunta: At Vireo, the team split its 2,000-line CLAUDE.md into testing.md, api-conventions.md, and deployment.md and placed the three files in .claude/commands/. Since then, CI reviews apply the API conventions only when someone happens to type /api-conventions in an interactive session, and the root CLAUDE.md is now nearly empty. What is the flaw in this implementation?
opcoes: The topic files need a paths field in their frontmatter, because files in .claude/commands/ load automatically only when a matching file is edited.
The split itself is the flaw: conventions should stay in one CLAUDE.md, because Claude Code reads only a single instruction file for each project.
That folder turns each file into a command someone must type; standing conventions split by topic go in .claude/rules/ so they load on their own.
CI runs Claude Code with -p, which reads CLAUDE.md but not files under .claude/, so the topic files must be pasted back into CLAUDE.md for CI.
questoes.explicacao: The .claude/rules/ directory is the alternative to a monolithic CLAUDE.md: it organizes topic-specific rule files that Claude Code loads as instructions. Files in .claude/commands/ become slash commands that only run when invoked, so the conventions dropped out of the automatic context. Moving the files to .claude/rules/ keeps the modular split and restores the conventions.
feedbacks: paths frontmatter belongs to rule files in .claude/rules/; commands are never auto-loaded, with or without it.
Claude Code supports modular instructions through .claude/rules/, @import, and directory-level files; splitting was a good idea, only the location is wrong.
Correct. Topic-specific instruction files go in .claude/rules/; .claude/commands/ is for slash commands.
CLAUDE.md and rules provide project context for CI runs as well; moving everything back would undo a useful split for no reason.

questoes.pergunta: At Vireo, the platform team added .claude/rules/terraform.md with YAML frontmatter paths: ["infra/terraform/**/*"]. A developer who spent a whole session editing only Kotlin files in services/catalog/ asked Claude about the team's resource tagging conventions, got a generic answer, and reported the rule file as broken. Later, in a session where Claude edited infra/terraform/cdn/main.tf, the tagging conventions were applied correctly. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: This is the intended behavior: the file's glob did not match anything Claude touched in the Kotlin session, so those conventions were never brought in.
The rule is misconfigured: files in .claude/rules/ load at session start, so a paths field that limits loading means the frontmatter is being ignored.
The rule loads only in sessions launched from inside infra/terraform/, so developers must start Claude Code from that directory for it to apply.
The rule loads only after a Terraform file has been committed during the session, so uncommitted edits to .tf files do not yet trigger it.
questoes.explicacao: A .claude/rules/ file with a paths field in its YAML frontmatter is conditional: it loads only when Claude works with files matching its glob. In the Kotlin-only session no Terraform file was touched, so the rule was correctly left out of context, which saves tokens and avoids irrelevant conventions. When Claude edited main.tf, the rule loaded as designed.
feedbacks: Correct. Path-scoped rules activate only for files that match their paths glob; that is the intended behavior.
Rules without paths load at session start, but a paths field deliberately makes loading conditional; nothing is ignored.
Confuses path-scoped rules with directory-level CLAUDE.md; activation depends on the files being edited, not where the session started.
Loading has nothing to do with commits; editing a matching file is enough, as the main.tf session shows.

questoes.pergunta: At Vireo, developers use several project skills in interactive Claude Code sessions while preparing PRs for CI. They report that after some skills run, the main session fills with output and later answers lose track of earlier decisions. Which TWO skills should set context: fork in their SKILL.md frontmatter? Choose TWO.
opcoes: /analyze-deps, which walks the module graph and prints a long dependency report before returning a short list of risky upgrades.
/format-changelog, which rewrites the CHANGELOG entry for the current change and shows the final text for the developer to approve.
/brainstorm-tests, which explores many alternative test strategies for the current change before recommending the two that fit it best.
/explain-diff, which walks through the current change with the developer and answers follow-up questions about each modified file.
/fix-lint, which applies small lint fixes to the files in the current change so that the developer can review each diff in the session.
questoes.explicacao: context: fork runs a skill in an isolated sub-agent context so that its verbose output or exploratory reasoning does not pollute the main conversation; only the result returns. The dependency analysis (verbose output) and the test brainstorming (exploratory context) are the classic cases. Skills whose value lies in the main session, such as reviewing diffs, approving text, or answering follow-ups, should stay in it.
feedbacks: Correct. Verbose analysis output belongs in a forked context, with only the short list returned.
Short output that the developer approves in the session; forking adds nothing and hides the interaction.
Correct. Exploratory brainstorming is a classic case for context: fork; only the recommendation returns to the session.
Needs the ongoing conversation for follow-up questions; a forked context would lose that continuity.
The developer wants to see each diff in the session, so isolating the skill would hide exactly what they need.

questoes.pergunta: At Vireo, the CI test-generation job runs one claude -p session that writes tests for a PR and then, in the same session, is asked to "review the tests you just wrote and fix any weaknesses." The review step rarely changes anything, yet mutation testing later shows that 35% of the generated tests would not catch a real bug. There is no budget for human review of generated tests, and the fix must stay inside the automated pipeline. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Hand the code and the new tests to a second claude -p call that never saw how they were written, so that the review starts without that reasoning.
Keep the review in the same session but enable extended thinking for that step, so that Claude reasons more deeply about weaknesses in its own tests.
Keep the review in the same session but have Claude adopt a skeptical reviewer persona, so that it questions its earlier choices more aggressively.
Generate the tests twice in independent sessions and keep only tests that appear in both runs, so that weak tests produced by one run are filtered out.
questoes.explicacao: A model reviewing its own work in the same session retains the reasoning that produced it, so it is unlikely to question those decisions. An independent instance without the generator's reasoning context catches more issues than self-review instructions or extended thinking. Running the review as a separate invocation fits the automated pipeline and costs little.
feedbacks: Correct. An independent review instance without the generation context is more effective than self-review.
Extended thinking in the same session still reasons from the generator's context; an independent review is more effective.
A persona is still self-review; the session keeps the reasoning that justified the weak tests.
Agreement between runs does not measure test quality; two runs can produce the same weak assertion, and good tests may appear only once.

questoes.pergunta: At Vireo, the automated review produces about 25 findings on large PRs, but senior reviewers can triage only about 8 per PR. The team wants to route each finding to one of three destinations: posted directly, sent to the senior queue, or held for the weekly audit. Which TWO practices should the routing rely on? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Have three independent instances review the PR and route only findings reported by all three, so that the senior queue receives consensus findings.
Set the score cut-offs by checking them against past findings already labeled valid or invalid, so each band has a known hit rate.
Add a verification pass in which the model looks at each finding again and attaches a confidence score, so that the score decides where it goes.
Ask the model, in the same session that produced the findings, to double-check them, so that it confirms or withdraws each one before routing.
Post only the findings the model rates as high confidence and drop the rest, so that developers see fewer comments on each pull request.
questoes.explicacao: A verification pass in which the model reports a confidence score next to each finding provides a routing signal, and calibrating the thresholds against labeled past findings turns that signal into a known precision for each band. Together they send limited reviewer time where it matters most. Dropping low-confidence findings outright, same-session self-checks, and consensus voting each lose real issues or add bias.
feedbacks: Consensus voting suppresses real issues that only some runs catch, and it triples the cost.
Correct. Calibrating thresholds on labeled data makes the confidence bands meaningful.
Correct. Per-finding confidence from a verification pass enables routing by score.
Same-session self-review keeps the reasoning context that produced the findings, so it rarely withdraws its own mistakes.
Uses confidence to discard findings instead of routing them; real issues in the dropped set are lost and the audit destination is never used.

questoes.pergunta: At Vireo, a developer notices that Claude Code applies the rule "no raw SQL in controllers" on their laptop but ignores it in the team's cloud development container, even though both environments have the same commit of the repository checked out. The team is choosing how to diagnose this: (A) run /memory in a session in each environment and compare which memory files are loaded; (B) run git diff between the two checkouts to find a configuration file that differs. Which choice is best?
opcoes: Approach A, because the command lists the instruction files each session actually loaded, including any that live outside the repository.
Approach B, because Claude Code reads its instructions from the repository, so any difference in behavior has to come from files that git can see.
Approach A, but only on a CI runner, because CI starts from a clean environment and shows the configuration that developers should be loading.
Neither: reinstall Claude Code in the container, because a mismatched installation is the most common reason a loaded rule is not being applied.
questoes.explicacao: When behavior differs across sessions or environments, /memory shows which memory files each session has actually loaded, including user-level files such as ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md that live outside the repository. Comparing the two environments reveals the missing or extra file directly. git diff only covers versioned files, and the checkouts are identical.
feedbacks: Correct. /memory verifies which memory files are loaded and is the direct way to diagnose inconsistent behavior across sessions.
The checkouts are identical; the difference is likely a user-level file, such as ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, that git does not track.
The problem appears in the two developer environments; a CI runner cannot show what those sessions load differently.
Guesses at a cause without checking which instructions are loaded; /memory answers that directly.

questoes.pergunta: At Vireo, the rule file .claude/rules/e2e-tests.md has paths: ["web/player/e2e/**/*"]. The web team has since moved its end-to-end specs next to each feature, for example web/catalog/search/search.e2e.ts and web/account/billing/billing.e2e.ts, and new feature folders appear every month. Tests generated in those folders ignore the e2e conventions. The conventions must apply to every end-to-end spec, wherever it lives. What should you change?
opcoes: Add a CLAUDE.md to each feature folder that contains e2e specs, so that the conventions load whenever Claude edits files inside those folders.
Change the rule's paths to ["**/*.e2e.ts"], so that the conventions are loaded for spec files by their name pattern rather than by folder.
Remove the paths field from the rule's frontmatter, so that the conventions load in every session and apply to every file in the repository.
Move the e2e conventions into the CI prompt for the test-generation job, so that they are applied every time the pipeline generates tests.
questoes.explicacao: Glob patterns in a rule's paths can target files by type regardless of directory, so **/*.e2e.ts matches every end-to-end spec now and in future folders. Directory-level CLAUDE.md files must be added for each new folder, removing paths loads the conventions everywhere, and a CI-only prompt misses tests written in local sessions.
feedbacks: Directory-bound files must be copied into every new feature folder, which the monthly growth makes hard to keep up with.
Correct. A file-type glob applies the conventions to every matching spec wherever it lives.
Loads e2e conventions for unrelated work, wasting context and risking their application to non-test files.
Covers only the CI job; tests written in developers' interactive sessions would still miss the conventions.

questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Kestrel Industrial, an industrial IoT company that monitors pumps and compressors at customer plants, is building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents such as field service reports, calibration certificates, and supplier datasheets, validates the output with JSON schemas, and feeds the company's asset management platform, so it must handle edge cases gracefully and keep accuracy high. The extraction agent has three tools: extract_calibration ("Extracts calibration data"), extract_service_report ("Extracts report data"), and extract_datasheet ("Extracts datasheet data"). Calibration certificates attached as appendices to service reports go to extract_service_report in 31% of cases, and datasheets that include factory test results often go to extract_calibration. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The three schemas share many field names, so the model cannot tell from the input schemas alone which tool fits a document that mixes content types.
The system prompt has no few-shot examples of mixed documents, so the model has never seen which tool to choose when content types are combined.
tool_choice is set to "auto", so the model is free to pick among the extraction tools instead of being directed to the one that matches each document.
Each tool is explained in three words that never say what it accepts or where its scope ends, so the model has almost nothing to separate them by.
questoes.explicacao: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism the model uses to select tools. One-line labels such as "Extracts report data" do not explain which document types each tool handles, what inputs it expects, or how to treat a certificate embedded in a report, so selection among similar tools becomes unreliable. Expanding the descriptions addresses the root cause before adding examples or changing schemas.
feedbacks: Overlapping fields add some ambiguity, but the model relies mainly on descriptions; schemas were never meant to carry selection guidance on their own.
Few-shot examples could help with edge cases, but they add tokens without fixing the primary signal, which is the minimal descriptions.
"auto" lets the model choose a tool, which is intended here; forcing one tool would not tell it which document type it is looking at.
Correct. Minimal descriptions make selection among similar tools unreliable, because descriptions are the primary selection mechanism.

questoes.pergunta: At Kestrel Industrial, after extraction moved to tool use with a strict JSON schema, JSON parse failures fell from 3.2% to zero. However, the asset platform still rejects 2.7% of calibration records: some as-found readings land in the as_left field, and some measurement points report a deviation that does not equal the reading minus the reference value. The team lead says the schema now guarantees correct records. Which TWO statements are correct? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Making every field required would remove the remaining errors, because the model could no longer leave out or misplace any of the readings.
The remaining rejections show the schema is not really strict, because a strict schema would also stop values from landing in the wrong field.
Tool use with a strict schema removes malformed output, but it says nothing about whether a reading sits in the right field or adds up.
Asking for JSON in the response text instead of tool use would let the model reason more freely and so reduce these semantic errors.
Checks such as recomputing each deviation are still needed for every record after the schema-valid output arrives from the model.
questoes.explicacao: Tool use with a strict JSON schema guarantees syntactically valid, schema-compliant output, but it does not prevent semantic errors such as values in the wrong field or numbers that do not agree. Those require validation after extraction, such as recomputing deviations, ideally feeding a retry with the specific error. Making fields required or dropping tool use would not address semantic correctness.
feedbacks: Required fields do not stop misplacement, and they push the model to fabricate values when a reading is genuinely absent.
A schema checks types and structure, not meaning; a reading in the wrong field is perfectly valid JSON.
Correct. Strict schemas eliminate syntax errors but not semantic errors such as misplaced values.
Giving up tool use brings back syntax errors without making values any more correct.
Correct. Semantic validation, such as recomputing deviations, is still required after schema-valid extraction.

questoes.pergunta: At Kestrel Industrial, the prompt for maintenance work orders has detailed instructions for choosing a failure_mode (bearing, seal, electrical, lubrication, other). Clear cases are fine, but ambiguous ones such as "pump tripped on overcurrent after a seal leak flooded the motor" got "seal" on one run and "electrical" on another. The team added three examples of ambiguous work orders, each explaining why the root failure mode was chosen over the plausible alternative, and consistency on ambiguous cases rose from 61% to 89%. Which statement about this result is correct?
opcoes: The examples demonstrated how to settle a borderline case and why the rejected label did not fit, which written rules had not managed to get across.
The examples worked because they lengthened the prompt, and longer prompts make the model more deterministic, so other added guidance would have helped similarly.
The examples helped only for the three cases shown, so further gains will require adding an example for each ambiguous combination seen in production.
The examples work as a lookup table, so the model now copies the label of the closest example rather than reasoning about each work order.
questoes.explicacao: Few-shot examples are especially valuable for ambiguous cases: by showing the reasoning for choosing one option over a plausible alternative, they teach a judgment that detailed instructions alone did not convey, and the model can apply it to combinations it has not seen. The gain comes from demonstrated reasoning, not from prompt length or exact matching.
feedbacks: Correct. Few-shot examples demonstrate how to handle ambiguous cases and why one choice beats the plausible alternative.
Length is not the mechanism; the detailed instructions were already long and still produced inconsistent labels.
Few-shot examples let the model generalize the demonstrated judgment; an example for every combination is unnecessary.
Copying the nearest example would not improve consistency on new cases; the examples taught reasoning, not a table.

questoes.pergunta: At Kestrel Industrial, every extracted field currently goes to human review before reaching the asset platform, and reviewers are falling behind. The team proposes having the model output a confidence score from 0 to 1 for each extracted field and automatically accepting fields scored 0.85 or higher, sending everything else to review. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Reject it, because model-reported confidence is not a meaningful signal, so every field should keep going to human review regardless of its score.
Accept it with a change: pick the cut-off by testing the per-field scores against fields whose correct values are already known.
Accept it as proposed, because 0.85 already leaves a wide margin, so the fields scored above it are very likely to have been extracted correctly.
Accept it, but use a single document-level score instead, so that reviewers handle whole documents rather than individual extracted fields.
questoes.explicacao: Field-level confidence scores are useful for routing review attention, but only once they are calibrated: the threshold must be set using a labeled validation set so that a given score corresponds to a measured accuracy. A raw 0.85 cutoff is an assumption, not a measurement. Rejecting confidence outright discards a useful signal, and a document-level score hides which field is weak.
feedbacks: Overgeneralizes: uncalibrated confidence is unreliable, but calibrated field-level confidence is a sound way to route review.
Correct. Calibrate field-level confidence thresholds on a labeled validation set before using them to route review.
An uncalibrated threshold assumes the model's scores match its accuracy; that has to be measured first.
A document-level score loses the field granularity that tells reviewers where to look, and it still needs calibration.

questoes.pergunta: At Kestrel Industrial, the extraction system also raises anomaly flags on calibration certificates for the quality team, such as out-of-tolerance readings, missing signatures, and expired reference standards. The prompt says: "Only flag anomalies you are highly confident about. Be conservative." Still, 45% of flags are dismissed as false. The budget rules out adding a second model pass. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Spell out the exact condition that counts for each kind of anomaly, such as a reading beyond the certificate's tolerance, so that flags follow it.
Strengthen the wording to "flag only anomalies you are certain about" and repeat it at the end of the prompt, so that the model applies a stricter bar.
Ask the model for a confidence score on each anomaly and drop those below 0.8, so that only the strongest candidates reach the quality team's queue.
Set an explicit limit of two anomaly flags per certificate, so that the quality team's queue shrinks and the model keeps only its most important ones.
questoes.explicacao: General instructions such as "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings" do not improve precision, because the model still has no concrete definition of an anomaly. Explicit categorical criteria, such as what counts as out of tolerance and which signatures are required, tell it what to report and what to skip. Stronger wording, confidence cutoffs, and caps leave the definition vague.
feedbacks: Correct. Specific categorical criteria improve precision where general caution does not.
Stronger vague wording is still vague; it fails for the same reason as the current instruction.
Confidence-based filtering replaces criteria with an unreliable threshold and can drop real anomalies along with false ones.
An arbitrary cap drops real anomalies on bad certificates and keeps false ones on good certificates.

questoes.pergunta: At Kestrel Industrial, customer contracts require every field service report to be extracted and available in the asset platform within 40 hours of upload. Extraction runs on the Message Batches API, whose batches can take up to 24 hours. Today one batch is submitted every day at midnight, so a report uploaded at 00:30 can take more than 47 hours. The team wants to keep the batch savings. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Move all extraction to the synchronous API, so that reports are processed within minutes and the 40-hour commitment is met with a wide margin.
Keep the daily submission but split it into several smaller batches sent together at midnight, so that each of the smaller batches completes faster.
Submit a batch every 12 hours, so that a report waits at most 12 hours and, with up to 24 hours of processing, still lands within the 40-hour limit.
Keep the daily batch but move its submission to noon, so that reports uploaded during the working day are submitted sooner after they arrive.
questoes.explicacao: With up to 24 hours of batch processing and a 40-hour SLA, a report can wait at most 16 hours before submission; submitting every 12 hours keeps the worst case at 36 hours and leaves time for validation and loading. Submission frequency has to be derived from the SLA and the processing window. Smaller batches have no faster guarantee, a shifted daily batch still allows long waits, and going synchronous gives up the savings.
feedbacks: Meets the SLA but gives up the 50% savings the team wants to keep; matching submission frequency to the SLA achieves both.
The batch API has no latency guarantee for smaller batches, and reports uploaded after midnight still wait almost a full day.
Correct. Derive the submission window from the SLA minus the 24-hour processing window.
Shifting a single daily window only moves the worst case; a report uploaded at 12:30 still waits about 24 hours before submission.

questoes.pergunta: At Kestrel Industrial, the extraction agent has grown to 19 tools: six extraction schemas, unit converters, four registry lookups, three asset platform writers, an email notifier, an OCR retry tool, and a translator. Wrong-tool calls now occur in 14% of documents, mostly between neighboring tools. The team is choosing between two designs: (A) keep one agent with all 19 tools and rewrite every description in detail; (B) give the extraction agent only the five tools its role needs and move writing and notifications to a separate step with its own small tool set. Which choice is best?
opcoes: Design A, because descriptions are the primary selection mechanism, so detailing all 19 of them fixes misrouting without restructuring the system.
Design B, because the model chooses far more reliably among a handful of role-relevant tools than among 19, however well each one is described.
Design A with tool_choice set to "any", so that the model has to call one of the 19 tools rather than answer a document in plain text.
Design B, but give each agent all 19 tools with role-specific prompts, so that any agent can handle an unexpected document without a handoff.
questoes.explicacao: Giving one agent too many tools, such as 19 instead of 4 or 5, degrades selection reliability by increasing decision complexity, even with good descriptions. Scoping each agent to the tools its role needs reduces the options at each decision and prevents misuse of tools outside its specialization. Better descriptions help but do not remove the complexity of choosing among 19.
feedbacks: Better descriptions are worthwhile, but they do not offset the decision complexity of choosing among 19 tools, many of them unrelated to extraction.
Correct. Scoped tool sets reduce decision complexity and improve selection reliability.
"any" guarantees a tool call but does nothing to help the model pick the right one of 19.
Restores the 19-tool problem in every agent; role prompts do not reduce the number of options the model must weigh.

questoes.pergunta: At Kestrel Industrial, the system raises quality findings on calibration certificates, such as "reference standard expired" or "reading out of tolerance," which metrology reviewers accept or dismiss. The dismissal rate is 31%. Each month the team must report which document constructs drive dismissals, for example tolerances written as percentages instead of absolute values, so it can target prompt fixes. Findings currently have {certificate_id, field, message, severity}. What should you change?
opcoes: Add a free-text reasoning field to each finding, so that reviewers can read why the model raised it before they decide whether to dismiss it.
Add a confidence field to each finding and hide findings below 0.7, so that fewer weak findings reach reviewers and the dismissal rate goes down.
Add a dismissal_reason field that reviewers must fill in, so that the team can read through the reasons each month to find recurring problems.
Add a detected_pattern field to each finding, so that the monthly report can count dismissals per triggering construct instead of rereading cases.
questoes.explicacao: A detected_pattern field records which document construct triggered each finding, so dismissals can be aggregated by pattern and false positive sources identified systematically. Free-text reasoning or reviewer comments must be read one by one and do not reliably name the construct. Hiding low-confidence findings lowers the rate without explaining it.
feedbacks: Reasoning helps individual reviews, but free text is hard to aggregate and does not reliably identify the triggering construct.
Hides findings instead of explaining dismissals; the team still could not tell which constructs cause false positives.
Adds reviewer work, and free-text reasons rarely name the document construct consistently enough to group them.
Correct. detected_pattern lets dismissals be analyzed systematically by the construct that triggered them.

questoes.pergunta: At Kestrel Industrial, a nightly Message Batches job extracts specifications from about 3,000 supplier datasheets. Each request's custom_id is a running sequence number, and the loader matches each result to an asset record using the pump model number that Claude extracted from the datasheet. About 4% of records in the asset platform now show another model's specifications, concentrated in datasheets that cover several model variants in one table. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: Records are matched on a value Claude extracted, so a misread model number misplaces the record; custom_id should carry the record's ID.
Datasheets covering several variants are too similar to one another, so the model mixed specifications across requests processed in the same batch.
Sequential custom_id values are reused by the API across nights, so results from an earlier batch are sometimes returned for the current night's requests.
Multi-variant datasheets exceed the batch processing window, so the API returns partial results that the loader completes with the nearest model's data.
questoes.explicacao: custom_id exists to correlate each batch request with its response. Here it carries a meaningless sequence number, so the loader falls back on a value from the model's own output, and any extraction slip on a multi-variant datasheet also attaches the specifications to the wrong asset. Setting custom_id to the asset record ID makes correlation independent of extraction accuracy; the misread itself is a separate extraction issue.
feedbacks: Correct. Use custom_id with a meaningful key to correlate batch requests and responses instead of relying on extracted content.
Requests in a batch are independent; one datasheet's content cannot leak into another's response.
custom_id values are set by you and come back with each result of that batch; the API does not mix results across batches.
Processing time does not produce partial records filled from other models; the error comes from how results are matched to records.

questoes.pergunta: At Kestrel Industrial, the extraction agent has two well-described tools: extract_calibration_certificate, for lab certificates with as-found and as-left readings, and extract_service_report, for technicians' field reports. The system prompt also says: "Whenever a document mentions calibration, use extract_calibration_certificate." Field service reports that include a line such as "sensor recalibrated on site" are sent to the certificate tool 22% of the time. Which TWO actions should the team take? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Look through the system prompt for lines that tie a tool to a word, so that they can be rephrased in terms of the kind of document being processed.
Delete the "mentions calibration" line, so that the existing descriptions of the two tools decide which one a document needs.
Rename extract_calibration_certificate to extract_cert, so that the tool name no longer shares a word with the instruction in the system prompt.
Add few-shot examples of service reports that mention calibration, so that the model learns to override the keyword rule when the document is a report.
Add a routing step that scans each document for "calibration" before the model runs, so that service reports can be excluded by a second keyword.
questoes.explicacao: Keyword-sensitive instructions in the system prompt can create unintended tool associations that override well-written tool descriptions. The fix is to find such instructions and remove them or rewrite them in terms of document types, letting the descriptions do their job. Examples that fight the rule, cosmetic renames, and extra keyword routing keep the root cause in place.
feedbacks: Correct. Review system prompts for keyword-sensitive instructions that can override well-written tool descriptions.
Correct. Removing the keyword rule lets the well-written descriptions drive tool selection.
The trigger is the word in the document, not in the tool name; the instruction still fires on "calibration" in the report text.
Teaches the model to fight its own instructions; the conflicting keyword rule stays and keeps pulling reports to the wrong tool.
Adds a second brittle keyword layer on top of the first, and it will misroute any document that uses the words differently.

questoes.pergunta: At Kestrel Industrial, the extraction agent used a generic fetch_url tool to load supplier datasheets referenced in purchase records. Logs showed it also fetched a distributor's marketing pages, a forum thread, and firmware update archives. The team replaced it with load_supplier_document, which accepts only URLs on the approved supplier portals and only PDF or HTML documents, and returns a validation error for anything else. Off-target fetches dropped to zero and datasheet field extraction improved. Which statement about this result is correct?
opcoes: The improvement came mainly from the new tool's more specific name, which made the model more careful, so renaming fetch_url would have worked as well.
The limit now lives inside the tool: off-portal or wrong-type requests fail with an error, so the agent's mistaken picks no longer bring in content.
The new tool works because the model no longer decides which URL to open, since the tool now locates the right datasheet for each record by itself.
The same result could have been reached with a system prompt rule listing the approved portals, since the model follows such allowlists consistently.
questoes.explicacao: Replacing a generic tool with a constrained alternative moves the boundary into the tool: load_supplier_document validates the URL and the document type, so off-target requests fail with a clear error instead of loading irrelevant content. The model still chooses what to request, but the tool limits what can succeed. A prompt allowlist is guidance the model can miss, and a rename alone changes nothing enforceable.
feedbacks: A clearer name may help selection, but it cannot stop the agent from fetching a forum thread; the validation does that.
Correct. A constrained tool that validates document URLs prevents the misuse that a generic fetch_url allows.
The tool still takes the URL the model chooses; it validates the request rather than finding documents on its own.
A prompt allowlist is probabilistic and the model can still request other URLs; the tool's validation is what makes the limit hold.

questoes.pergunta: At Kestrel Industrial, technicians' notes contain informal measurements such as "about 3 bar," "half a turn past snug," and "~1.5k rpm," and the extraction prompt uses four few-shot examples showing how to normalize them. Notes come from about 400 technicians at 30 plants, and new phrasings appear every week. An engineer proposes replacing the examples with a table of 120 exact phrases and their normalized values. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Accept it, because a table of exact phrases is deterministic, so each listed phrase is normalized the same way and errors become easy to trace.
Accept it, but keep one few-shot example to show the output format, so that the model applies the table and formats normalized values correctly.
Reject it, because the examples carry the reasoning behind each conversion, which the model can apply to wording that no list anticipated.
Reject it, and have technicians pick measurements from a fixed form, so that notes no longer contain informal phrasings that need normalization.
questoes.explicacao: Few-shot examples let the model generalize the judgment they demonstrate to new patterns, which matters when phrasings keep changing. A table only covers pre-specified phrases and leaves every new phrasing unhandled. Changing how 400 technicians write notes is a process change outside the extraction system and not a proportionate answer.
feedbacks: Determinism for listed phrases comes at the cost of failing on every new phrasing, and new ones arrive weekly.
Keeping the format example does not fix coverage; the table still cannot normalize phrasings it does not list.
Correct. Few-shot examples enable generalization to novel patterns rather than matching only pre-specified cases.
Pushes the burden onto technicians across 30 plants and does nothing for the notes that already exist.

questoes.pergunta: At Kestrel Industrial, the extraction agent has two tools: parse_equipment_doc ("Parses equipment documents and returns structured fields") and extract_asset_data ("Extracts structured data from asset documents"). One was built for OCR text from motor nameplates and the other for warranty certificates, but 27% of documents go to the wrong one. Which TWO changes would most directly fix the misrouting? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Rename them after what they read, such as extract_nameplate_fields and extract_warranty_terms, so the names stop sounding alike.
Make the two schemas more distinct by adding unique required fields to each, so that the model can tell them apart from parameters alone.
Merge both tools into one generic tool that returns the fields of both schemas, so that the model does not have to choose between the two.
Add a system prompt line telling the model to prefer extract_asset_data when unsure, so that ambiguous documents go to one default tool.
Rewrite both descriptions to state which document each accepts and what it returns, so that each says when to use the other tool instead.
questoes.explicacao: Near-identical names and descriptions are the cause of the misrouting. Renaming the tools to reflect their purpose and rewriting the descriptions to state inputs, outputs, and when to use the alternative removes the overlap. Merging into a do-everything tool, defaulting to one tool, or relying on schema differences leaves the model without a clear basis for choosing.
feedbacks: Correct. Renaming to remove functional overlap makes each tool's purpose clear.
Required fields that do not apply to a document push the model to fabricate values, and parameters are a weak selection signal.
Returning the fields of both schemas invites values in the wrong fields and hides which document type was processed.
A default only decides ties in one direction; documents of the other type still get misrouted whenever the model is unsure.
Correct. Descriptions that state inputs, outputs, and boundaries with the similar tool eliminate the overlap.

questoes.pergunta: At Kestrel Industrial, the system raises inconsistency findings on maintenance work orders, such as a part number missing from the bill of materials or labor hours above standard, and each finding already includes a detected_pattern value. Planners dismiss 41% of findings, but their decisions are recorded only as a weekly dismissal percentage on a dashboard. The team has rewritten the prompt every week based on a few complaints, and the rate swings between 33% and 47% with no trend. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Freeze the prompt and collect two more months of the weekly dismissal rate, so that the team has a stable baseline before making further changes.
Add the latest planner complaints as few-shot examples of findings to avoid, so that the prompt reflects the cases planners dismissed most recently.
Change the instruction to "only report inconsistencies you are confident about," so that weaker findings are dropped before planners see them.
Log every accept or dismiss against the pattern that produced the finding, so that the team can see which patterns are rejected most.
questoes.explicacao: A feedback loop needs to connect each dismissal to the construct that triggered the finding. With decisions logged against detected_pattern, the team can see which patterns produce most dismissals and fix those systematically instead of reacting to anecdotes. An aggregate weekly rate cannot show where the false positives come from.
feedbacks: A stable aggregate baseline still cannot show which patterns cause dismissals, so the next change would remain a guess.
Continues the anecdote-driven cycle that produced the swings; a few complaints may not represent the main sources of dismissal.
Vague confidence wording does not improve precision and would hide findings without revealing which patterns are the problem.
Correct. Tracking dismissals by detected_pattern enables systematic analysis of where false positives come from.

questoes.pergunta: At Kestrel Industrial, an extraction subagent and a validation subagent work under a coordinator. For 70% of calibration certificates, the extraction subagent needs to confirm that the instrument's serial number exists in the asset registry; each check now goes back through the coordinator to the validation subagent, adding two round trips and about 35% more processing time. The validation subagent has seven tools, some of which write to the registry. Which design is best?
opcoes: Give the extraction subagent the seven validation tools, so that it can complete registry checks itself without returning control to the coordinator.
Give extraction a single read-only serial lookup tool for this frequent check, so that the other validation work still goes through the coordinator.
Merge the extraction and validation subagents into one agent with both tool sets, so that the registry check happens inside a single shared context.
Load the full asset registry into the extraction subagent's prompt, so that it can check serial numbers against it without making tool calls.
questoes.explicacao: Scoped tool access gives each agent only the tools its role needs, plus limited cross-role tools for specific high-frequency needs. A single read-only lookup_serial tool removes the round trips for the 70% case while complex validation stays with the validation subagent through the coordinator. Handing over all seven tools or merging the agents expands the tool set and exposes write access.
feedbacks: Over-provisions the extraction subagent with write-capable tools outside its role, raising the risk of misuse.
Correct. A scoped cross-role tool covers the high-frequency need while complex cases still go through the coordinator.
Merging creates one agent with a large tool set, which degrades selection and removes the separation between roles.
A full registry in the prompt consumes context on every request and goes stale; a lookup tool is the proportionate fix.
